author: Autodesk
description: MPM snow simulation that shows dynamic activation of points using an infection solver
documentation:
## Snow Activation Graph

### Description

This graph shows how to use the MPM solver to simulate artistically activated snow sourced from a helix mesh.

The MPM solver has a couple of new capabilities that this graph demonstrates. The `source_mpm_snow` compound has a new parameter called `passthrough_points`. This allows the point position of existing points to be used as the initial position of the snow. To facilitate animated activation there is another parameter called `passthrough_properties`. Once the property name `point_active` is entered in the `passthrough_properties` parameter, the solver will update the property on the input points.

The activation of the snow is driven by the `animated_activation` compound which contains the `basic_infection` compound. `basic_infection` is documented as a standalone browser graph - see the point_infection graph that is part of the Scatter Pack in the Bifrost Browser. The infection activation portion of the graph is done on a very low number of points for speed. This 'proxy' result is then used to create a volume containing the property used to drive activation - `voxel_emit` which was originally a property on the points driven by the `basic_infection` compound.

As mentioned earlier, the `passthrough_points` parameter is enabled on the `source_mpm_snow` compound. This does mean that the user is responsible for creating the points to be used in the MPM solve in the graph before the simulation. This would have been more difficult in past version, however, a new node exists called `mpm_settings_to_scatter_density`. This node takes an input of `mpm_solver_settings` and is used to calculate the output value of `density_amount` which is wired into the `amount` port of `scatter_points`. Now that the points are created in the graph, they are able to have the `point_active` property driven inside of the `point_activation` compound.

### Inputs, Controls & Outputs

A mesh input is the driver for this example. In theory, any other mesh that can be voxelized could be used instead of the supplied helix. However, the most important thing to consider is the world scale. The scene may need extensive tweaking of the size of the input mesh is drastically different than the helix. A world space starting position also needs to be defined inside of the `animated_activation` compound, so keep that in mind as well. It's not completely procedural at the moment and a starting point would likely be art-directed.

There are two `if` nodes in the graph. One is named 'preview_quality_resolution'. There are two `value` nodes that are wired into the inputs. The output value drives the `detail_size` parameter of the `mpm_solver_settings` compound. The output is also used during the meshing stage. This setup allows you to switch from a preview resolution to a production quality resolution with a single click. The other `if` node named 'small_region_for_fast_sim' switches between two `create_mesh_cube` nodes with varying sizes. The smaller cube is used to severely restrict the simulation region. The rationale for this additional workflow is to quickly switch to a fast solve in a limited volume to preview full resolution MPM and dial in the material properties. Both `if` nodes can allow very quick iterations which can be essential during tight turnarounds.

The output of this graph is a mesh ready to be rendered with Arnold. The points from the MPM simulation have been converted into a levelset, then converted to a polygon mesh. The example also includes a `standard_surface_mat` that is wired into an `assign_material` node to define a snow material for the mesh. The snow material utilizes subsurface scattering and a shiny coat to approximate an icy snow. While a volume could also be used to represent the snow, in this case the snow benefitted from a specular highlight found on a hard surface material.

### Workflow and Tips

The full resolution simulation, meshing, and rendering takes time. The simulation is about 2 hours at production quality and frames were rendered in around 5 minutes apiece at 720p. While this is pretty reasonable for production quality simulation and render, that would take too long to iterate when initially building the effect and dialing in the behavior. Building on the idea of having the `if` nodes to drive preview quality and bounds, there are other parameters to tweak as well. The MPM solver does quite a good job at remaining fairly consistent at various resolutions. It is best to work out timing and rough material properties at a preview resolution and slowly increase the resolution to get accurate collisions and more details in the material. While increasing the particles per voxel will give more snow particle details, there does need to be a small enough detail size to handle self collisions nicely. The `vibration_speed` property on the `source_mpm_snow` node has a substantial effect on the solver speed. Lower values can greatly help to increase iterations, but at a 'cost'- the resulting simulation will have a very bouncy quality. This can be an acceptable tradeoff when developing the simulation, then increase the `vibration_speed` only as high as it needs to be - for snow a value around 50 is ideal. During preview iterations, 20 was sufficient for initial tests. Finally, setting a very small simulation bound is a great way to dial in look of the material at production quality. Once that small region is looking good it's a great time to switch back to the full bounds an ensure the full simulation is behaving as expected.

The `file_cache` compound is not required. However, it is strongly recommended to cache out the MPM particles. Do note for efficiency there is an `erase_component_properties` compound before the `file_cache` compound to reduce the file size as many properties are not required outside of the simulation. It also makes it very easy to iterate on the meshing and render settings without having to worry about losing a simulation result once everything is dialed in. Also, once cached, the rendering could be easily distributed to a render farm if that is available.

metadata.description: MPM snow simulation that shows dynamic activation of points using an infection solver

_notes.text:
The detail size for MPM is set to a preview quality. This enables quick simulation to achieve the desired activation behavior without spending too much time on the solve while the timing is being refined.
Unchecking the box for the preview resolution control above will enable a production quality example which will take longer to compute, use more RAM, and produce a more compelling result.

Another strategy to iterate quickly and achieve a desired result is to severely limit the simulation bounds. This small volume allows one to view results at the higher detail level in a small area to dial in material properties without simulating the entire scene.

Render settings:

On the Bifrost shape node, it is ideal that one set:
Arnold --> Translator Options --> Motion blur mode: Velocity Only

This ensures the quickest translate time since the renderer will only be able to use the point_velocity property stored on the mesh.

Arnold:

AA - 7
Diffuse - 2
Specular - 2
Transmission - 1
SSS - 2
Volume Indirect - 1

Adaptive Sampling (Enable)
Max Camera AA - 16

Motion Blur (Enable)

The resulting mesh benefited from an increased resolution compared to the MPM simulation.

The point_size is divided by 2 to have small grains that break off of the larger snow chunks.

Similarly, the points are being converted to a volume at 3.5x the resolution of the MPM simulation. This ensures that the there is ample resolution on the render mesh to represent single droplets that have broken off of the simulation.

The file_cache is set to passthrough.
When running the simulation at production resolution it is ideal to cache out the simulation data before rendering, as typically the render will take longer than the simulation and can be easily resumed (unlike the simulation)

The basic_infection compound is from the Bifrost Browser --> Scatter Pack --> point_infection

See the browser graph itself for further details.

This basic infection graph is used simulate property growth on a set of points. It's a weighted-average by distance system that can mimic the spread of an infection in a medium. It's build around a solver, so you will need to reset the solver by returning to a frame before the start_frame listed on the compound.

object_to_infect

The points object input. Points object only.

Point Generation

  • Infection Points:
    The number of initial infected points.
  • Random Seed:
    Seed for the random number generator that chooses the initial infection points.
  • Use Custom Infection Points:
    Instead of using the internal seed points generator, the solver reads the point positions from the custom_seed_positions input. custom_seed_positions is a float3 input and can be connected to internal bifrost values or float3 values passed in from your scene.

Infection Settings

  • Infection Property:
    The name of the main infection property, this will grow across the frame range allowing it to be used to drive animations, scales, colors etc.
  • Normalized Infection Property:
    The same as above, but mapped to a 0-1 range.
  • Start Frame:
    The starting frame of the solver, The initial settings will be applied at frames below this number.
  • Initial Infection Value:
    Starting value of the Infection Property.
  • Neighbor Count:
    As the solver runs over the points, it looks for neighbors of the current point and reads their Infection Property values. This controls how many neighbors it looks at. This, combined with the Infection Spread property, controls how fast the infection propogates.
  • Infection Spread:
    This is the radius in which the solver looks for point infection values. Higher values can cause the solver to slow down. This, combined with the Neighbor Count property, controls how fast the infection propogates.
  • Infection Intensity:
    This controls how much of the distance between points is taken into account. It has the effect of controlling how fast the intensity of the infection grows.
  • Additional Infection Points:
    Add n additional new infection points. This adds new infection points on every step of the solver. This is useful in the situation where your infection must be total.
  • Additional Infection Frame:
    Allows you to set the frame after which the new infection points are added.
  • Max Infection Value:
    The highest your infection intensity can be.

Diagnostic

  • Point Size:
    Point size on screen.
  • Show Radius Sample:
    When switched on, it will display the Infection Spread as a circle. This is the radius that the solver looks in to find neighbors. Only shows this on the starting points.
  • Infection Color:
    All uninfected points always are drawn as black. Anything with an infection property above zero will be drawn in this color.
  • Intensity Color:
    As the intensity of the infection grows, the color of the point will grow to be this color.

Outputs

  • All Points:
    Outputs all the points with properties
  • Infected Points:
    Outputs only the points with an infection value above zero
